passage: You want a story, mone? Then your grandpa Joseph will tell you about your Aunt Jaya when she was nine. First week at the new school in Kochi, she walked up to a girl sitting alone at lunch and asked, "Can I share your mat?" By Friday they were a pair. Then came a fight over whose turn it was on the swing, and both of them stomped home. Next morning Jaya went straight to her teacher and said, "We had a fight and I don't know how to fix it. Can you help?" No hiding, no sulking for weeks. The teacher sat them together, and by the end of lunch they were laughing about the swing. That evening Jaya told me, "She wasn't being mean, Pappa. She just wanted a turn too."

qa.q: What did Jaya ask the girl sitting alone at lunch?
qa.a: She asked, "Can I share your mat?"

qa.q: What does Jaya's remark "She just wanted a turn too" suggest about how she thinks about others?
qa.a: It suggests she feels no lasting anger toward her friend; she believes the girl meant no harm, so she can let the quarrel go.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make the morning after the swing fight, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She went to her teacher and asked for help to fix the fight rather than sulking, which let the friendship recover the same day.

qa.q: How might the girl who had been sitting alone have felt when Jaya came over?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and pleased to be invited, since by Friday the two of them were a pair.

grounding: A grandfather recalls his nine-year-old daughter making a friend, quarrelling, openly asking a teacher for help and assuming her friend meant well.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the museum shelter, and the bus would leave in ten minutes. Uma, ten, had lost the worksheet she and Rafiq were meant to hand in together. "You had it last!" Rafiq snapped. "I didn't mean to," Uma said, cheeks hot. For a second she wanted to hide behind the others. Instead she splashed across to Mrs Pillai. "Ma'am, we lost our sheet. Can we have another one?" Mrs Pillai handed her a spare, damp at the edges. Uma held it out to Rafiq. "Half each? You do the drawings, you're faster." He grinned, and the fight was gone. On the ride back they finished it on their knees, bumping elbows at every pothole.

qa.q: How long did Uma and Rafiq have before the bus left?
qa.a: The bus would leave in ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when Rafiq snapped at her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and stung; her cheeks went hot and for a second she wanted to hide.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Uma, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of hiding, she went to Mrs Pillai and asked for a new sheet, which solved the problem fast and gave her something to share with Rafiq.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Uma offered him the drawings?
qa.a: He likely felt included and appreciated, which is why his anger faded and he grinned. 🙂

grounding: Under time pressure in the rain, a ten-year-old asks a teacher for help without hiding and repairs a quarrel with her friend.

passage: Observation note, Class 4, week two. Salma joined us from another city only last Monday, yet by Wednesday she had walked up to the kho-kho group and asked, "Can I be on a team?" Today she and Abhinav argued over whose turn it was to chase; voices rose, and she stamped off to the steps. Ten minutes later she was back: "I think you thought it was yours. Let's toss for it." In maths she raised her hand twice and said plainly, "I don't get this bit." No blushing. I have paired her with Abhinav for the craft project; they are already bickering happily.

qa.q: What did Salma ask the kho-kho group?
qa.a: She asked, "Can I be on a team?"

qa.q: How can you tell Salma felt comfortable asking for help in maths?
qa.a: She raised her hand twice and plainly said she didn't get it, with no blushing, so she seemed confident rather than ashamed.

qa.q: What did Salma do after the argument that helped the friendship recover?
qa.a: She cooled off, came back, guessed Abhinav had meant no harm and suggested a toss, so both could keep playing.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Salma after the quarrel?
qa.a: Abhinav probably sees her as someone who can argue and still be fair, which makes it easy to keep working and even bickering together.

grounding: Shows a school-age child who joins in, recovers from a quarrel by assuming good intent and asks for help openly.

passage:
Tuesday. Vikas said I broke his bat on purpose. I didn't! It cracked on a full toss. I was so angry I went home without saying bye. At dinner I told Mummy everything and asked, "How do I fix it without looking like a baby?" She said just say what happened and offer to help. So after homework I went down with glue and tape. Vikas was sitting on the stairs, looking at the bat. He said, "Sorry I shouted. I think it was already cracked." We taped it together. It looks ugly but it works. Tomorrow we play again.
Hemant

qa.q: What did Hemant take down to the stairs after homework?
qa.a: Glue and tape.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Vikas said the bat was broken on purpose?
qa.a: Hemant felt angry and wrongly blamed, because the bat had cracked on a full toss, so Hemant went home without saying bye.

qa.q: What made it easier for Hemant to mend the quarrel?
qa.a: Asking Mummy for help openly, then going down with glue and tape and offering to fix the bat together.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas when Hemant turns up with glue and tape?
qa.a: Vikas, already sitting with the broken bat, gets an easy chance to say sorry too and admit it was already cracked, so the fight can end.

grounding: Illustrates a child who asks a parent for help without shame and repairs a friendship after a quarrel.

passage: Dust rose over the school ground in Khandwa as Darshan stepped over the line and the kabaddi match was lost. "You gave it away!" Varun yelled. Darshan kicked a stone and walked off towards the well. That evening Varun sat on his roof, still cross, but thinking. Darshan never lost on purpose, and he had been limping since morning. Next day Varun found him by the tea stall. "Your foot okay? Sorry I yelled." Then Varun went to the PT teacher and asked, without looking at his shoes, "Can you teach us to hold the line? We keep losing." Darshan grinned and came along.

qa.q: Where did Varun sit that evening?
qa.a: He sat on his roof, still cross, but thinking.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling on the roof, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: He was still cross about the lost match, but remembering that Darshan had been limping made him think Darshan never lost on purpose.

qa.q: Which choice helped most, and why?
qa.a: Saying sorry first and then asking the PT teacher for help together, because it repaired the friendship and gave both boys a way to improve.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when Varun asks about his foot?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels relieved and noticed, since his limp is finally seen and the yelling is taken back.

grounding: Shows a child who assumes a friend meant well, recovers after a quarrel and asks an adult for help without shame.

passage:
In a classroom in Osaka, Kaito and Clara were building a paper bridge for the science fair. Clara wanted arches; Kaito wanted triangles. "Your idea is boring," Clara snapped.
Kaito's cheeks went hot. He turned his back and glued triangles on his own.
At lunch he felt bad about it. He didn't think Clara hated him; she got cross fast and forgot fast.
After lunch he walked to the teacher's desk. "Mr Sato, we're stuck. Can you help us choose?"
Mr Sato suggested testing both. The arches held more coins.
Kaito shrugged and grinned. "Okay, yours wins. Can we put triangles on the sides?"
Clara laughed. "Deal." By home time they were arguing happily about paint colours.

qa.q: Which design held more coins?
qa.a: The arches held more coins.

qa.q: How did Kaito feel after turning his back on Clara, and what did he think about her?
qa.a: He felt bad about it, but he didn't think Clara hated him; he believed she got cross fast and forgot fast.

qa.q: Which of Kaito's choices helped them move on?
qa.a: He asked Mr Sato for help without feeling ashamed, then accepted the result and offered a way to include his idea.

qa.q: How might Clara see Kaito's offer to add triangles?
qa.a: Clara probably felt relieved that he wasn't holding a grudge after her snappy remark, so she laughed and agreed.

grounding: Shows a child who handles a quarrel, asks for help without shame, assumes good intent and recovers the friendship.
